title: Three Decades of Smart Noninvasive Older Adults Monitoring: Trends in Objectives, Privacy Preserving, Modality and AI Assistance
abstract: The aging population is growing rapidly, driving demand for effective, noninvasive monitoring solutions to support independent living and improve quality of life. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of noninvasive monitoring research of older adults from 1990 to 2024, covering 4,864 primary research articles retrieved from IEEE Xplore and ScienceDirect. A systematic methodology is utilized to classify studies by application orientation and analytical approach, followed by bibliometric and trend analyses. Research on noninvasive monitoring of older adults has shown steady fourfold growth over the past decades, reflecting increasing attention to smart, technology-driven aging care solutions. Keyword co-occurrence analysis revealed prominent themes, including artificial intelligence (AI), wearable technologies, IoT, and human activity recognition. Privacy-Preserving strategies have become a central focus, and AI-driven approaches have expanded rapidly since 2017. The majority of studies remain diagnostic-oriented, with only a very small portion explicitly targeting preventive monitoring. Overall, the field demonstrates rapid growth, diagnostic focus, privacy awareness, and increasing adoption of AI-assisted tools to support the aging population.

title: Transformer-based Deep Learning Framework for Intrusion Detection in Smart Grids
abstract: As smart grids grow in complexity and interconnectedness, they become susceptible to more cyber threats that can impact grid operations and have great financial implications. Traditional IDS systems have a hard time detecting new-generation cyber-attacks, especially the ones that are sophisticated or novel. We present a new Transformer-based deep learning model for real-time smart grid intrusion detection in this paper. Our model uses the Transformer for anomaly detection and an Autoencoder for unsupervised learning to identify deviations from regular grid performance. The performance of the model is tested on the CIC IDS Dataset, and it is shown that our approach leads to much better detection precision as compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. In particular, the proposed model provides 95% detection accuracy, improving 20% over traditional signature-based IDS, with a false positive rate improvement of 15%. Moreover, the system can detect both short-lived intrusions (over 10s of seconds) like burst power spikes and long-term attacks (e.g., data exfiltration with a much slower creep), rendering it practically flexible for dynamic and sophisticated cyber hazards. The solution is scalable, can work as part of smart grid infrastructure, and presents a resource-efficient, real-time, comprehensive response against cyberattacks.

venue: 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)
title: “We can't Allow IoT Vendors to Pass off all Such Liability to the Consumer”: Investigating the U.S. Legal Perspectives on Liability for IoT Product Security
abstract: As the regulatory landscape for the Internet of Things (IoT) evolves, vendors are moving towards certifying their products for security. Thus, we need to understand who is liable when certification failures result in harm, i.e., when certified products have vulnerabilities that are exploited to cause harm to users. This paper addresses the fundamental and timely question that has significant implications for vulnerability detection in certified products: who is liable for harm resulting from vulnerabilities in certified products, and who should be so liable? Through a qualitative analysis of contractual documents from 20 IoT vendors, this paper investigates how liability is currently defined in vendor-user contractual terms. This analysis then incorporates an expert survey of 18 legal professionals to examine their perspectives on liability within this context. Our analysis leads to 14 key findings (F1- F14) that show how vendors exclude liability to the maximum extent with (sometimes unlawful) exclusions, and how the perspectives of legal experts lie in stark contrast to what we observe in contracts (which are drafted by lawyers). We distill our findings into three key themes that call for a robust and clear liability framework, creating an incentive for IoT vendors to ensure that their IoT products meet proper security and privacy standards.

title: Understanding Consumer Trade-Offs in the Adoption of IoT Services: Privacy Concerns vs. Perceived Benefits in the Indian Context
abstract: As Internet of Things (IoT) technologies increasingly integrate into daily life, this study examines how Indian consumers evaluate the trade-offs between the perceived benefits of IoT services—such as utility, convenience, and enhanced experiences—and their concerns about personal data privacy. The research identifies how key innovation-related attributes (perceived advantage, ease of integration, and visibility of use) influence adoption intentions. Additionally, it explores the role of Privacy Self-Efficacy (PSE) in shaping individual confidence in managing privacy risks, thereby moderating the relationship between perceived value and willingness to adopt IoT-enabled services. This study proposes a conceptual framework informed by Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) theory and Social Exchange Theory (SET) to examine Indian consumers’ adoption of IoT services. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 700 Indian respondents who use or are aware of IoT-enabled products and services. To analyze the direct and moderating effects of key constructs, including Privacy Self-Efficacy, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) was utilized.

title: A Literature Review of Federated Learning Algorithms for Load Prediction
abstract: Load prediction is an essential task for optimizing energy distribution, reducing operational costs, and maintaining grid stability. However, traditional centralized approaches to training predictive models often encounter significant challenges related to privacy, scalability, and latency. As such, federated learning has emerged as a promising alternative by enabling collaborative model training across distributed nodes without direct data sharing, thereby preserving privacy. Therefore, this study presents a comprehensive literature review of federated learning algorithms that could be applied to load prediction, covering both established and emerging strategies such as EdgeFed, FedSGD, FedNorm, FLchain, FedAvg, FedYogi, FedAdam, and FedAdagrad. In addition, this work further examines several deep learning algorithms, namely RNN, LSTM, GRU, and TCN, that could be integrated with the federated learning algorithms. Through this analysis, the study synthesizes existing contributions, underscores unresolved challenges, and outlines opportunities for future research aimed at achieving a balance between accuracy, efficiency, and privacy in energy applications

title: Analysis of Blockchain-Integrated Access Control Models in Distributed Cloud Environments
abstract: widespread adoption of decentralized cloud applications has driven the requirement for secure, scalable, and auditable access control methods. Existing centralised methods, such as role-based, attribute-based, and required access control, suffer from a single point of failure, a lack of disclosure, and difficulties enforcing cross-language, cross-country policies. Blockchain has emerged as a breakthrough in overcoming these limitations by creating hand-in-hand decentralization and immutability, combined with programmable trust (smart contracts, decentralized identities). This paper addresses the basics of cloud access control and blockchain, along with the evolution of their integration in various fields, including healthcare, IoT, financial systems, smart grids, and cloud storage. An organized technique inspired by the systematic literature review principles is applied to review selected proposals, cluster access control models, and compare their performance with the classical models. Transparency, accountability, and automation of authorization are also validated, together with practical uses that illustrate that, in the context of compliance and resiliency, blockchain is of paramount importance. Open challenges, including scalability, privacy, interoperability, and regulatory issues, are analyzed in the review, as well as promising research directions such as lightweight consensus, cross-chain interoperability, and AI-blockchain integration. This work presents an overview of blockchain as an essential basis for secure access control for possible distributed cloud systems, incorporating the most recent trends and challenges.

venue: 2025 7th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Speech Technology (AIST)
title: Multi-Agent Systems for Collaborative and Distributed Decision-Making: Design and Applications
abstract: The hard distributed problems that no one agent or centralized system can solve are increasingly looked at problems that can be addressed using multi-agent systems. Independent agents collaborate with other independent agents pursuing either the same or similar objectives. Focusing on the basics and frontiers of MAS, this survey uses structures and mechanisms of coordination and communication as points of reference. First, we cover the routes of coordination and communication that are traditional: voting, negotiation, consensus, and auction, the most primary forms of agent interactions. Then, we cover the routes of coordination and communication that are contemporary: agent communication languages. Next, we look into the main architectural styles used in MAS: hierarchical, heterarchical, and holonic, along with newer hybrid methods and recent approaches based on large language models [2], all aimed at addressing certain orchestration challenges through global planning and local execution [1]. To display MAS realization, we present four representative domains: smart grids, autonomous transport, supply chains, and disaster response. In each domain, multiple agent teams come together—for instance, smart meters coordinate power consumption, self-driving vehicles negotiate route formation, factories adjust schedules for production, and rescue drones form coalitions—demonstrating both the opportunities and unique challenges posed by MAS. System-level challenges become prominent across these domains. Scalability to large agent populations, security and privacy in open networks, explainability of agent decisions, and conflict resolution are some of the major research challenges. Recent surveys observe that privacy-aware cybersecure multi-agent frameworks [3] and privacy-preserving consensus protocols should be developed.

venue: 2025 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Quantum Computation-Based Sensor Application (ICAIQSA)
title: Iterative and Empirical Models for Quantum Blockchain in IoT Security: A Systematic Review and Performance Analysis
abstract: With billions of resource-constrained devices exchanging sensitive data over heterogeneous networks, the fast-growing expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has heightened the concerns of security. In this regard, classical blockchain, despite its promise, has two main disadvantages: it cannot scale properly under massive IoT traffic and it can be vulnerable to quantum adversaries. This work attempts to fill these gaps through an analytical and empirical review of thirty recent models using blockchain, post-quantum cryptography, and quantum-native approaches. Conducted under the PRISMA guidelines, this review systematically examines how its models perform with respect to common security metrics: delay, complexity, throughput, security efficiency, and packet delivery ratio. The findings of the study suggest that regular adaptive blockchains with dynamic block size optimization and lightweight hashing consistently achieve high throughput (>900 Tx/sec) and packet delivery ratios (>95%) in IoT environments making them the most feasible solution in near term. In contrast, post-quantum models, using hybrid encryption and an optimized SIKE provide significantly enhanced resilience (security efficiency in the range of 92% to 96%) while introducing computational overhead unsuited for low-power devices. The frameworks of quantum blockchain, utilizing QKD-based authentication and heap-driven key distribution, provide unsurpassed security efficiency (>95%) but stay largely constrained experimentally at this stage. The synthesis from the empirical study suggests a multi-layered approach, consisting of immediate implementations of lightweight adaptive models, mid-term enhancements through post-quantum cryptography optimization, and a long-term aim of deployment of full quantum blockchain architecture. Such insights would prove pivotal in IoT sectors with real-time requirements like health, smart grids, and industrial automation, where balancing scalability, efficiency, and quantum resilience is of utmost importance. Hence, the work provides an avenue for foundational mapping of advancement in quantum-secure IoT ecosystems.

venue: 28th International Conference and Exhibition on Electricity Distribution (CIRED 2025)
title: Overview of smart meter use cases in the Netherlands
abstract: Balancing individual privacy with grid insight poses significant challenges, especially as the analysis of low voltage grid behaviour requires individual data, governed by strict privacy laws in the Netherlands. This paper demonstrates how this balance is maintained through intensive collaboration between privacy authorities and distribution system operators (DSOs) via "use cases." The aim of this paper is to provide an overview of approved use cases in the Netherlands and their benefits for DSOs. Following the liberalisation of the electricity market, the rollout of smart meters began in 2014, that resulted in approximately 90% of Dutch households are presently equipped with these devices. Initially, smart meter data was used solely for billing purposes, but a Code of Conduct approved in 2022 now enables its use for grid management under stringent privacy regulations. Within Netbeheer Nederland, a structured process ensures that each use case complies with privacy agreements and is approved by all DSOs. This paper outlines the methodologies and collaborations involved, highlighting the balance between data utility and privacy protection. The results showcase ten formalised use cases that enhance smart grid management while safeguarding individual privacy, demonstrating the successful integration of smart meter data in grid operations without compromising personal data security.

title: Lwe-Based Single Noisy Linear Equations for Public Key Over Integer Encryption
abstract: In this work, we introduce a novel post-quantum public key encryption scheme over integers, leveraging a hybrid approach that combines large random numbers with the Learning With Errors (LWE) system. The scheme addresses the security challenges posed by quantum computing advancements, aiming to provide a robust solution resistant to quantum-based attacks. By using the unknown random number hardness assumption with enhancements to the traditional LWE framework and operating directly on integers, this approach ensures a high level of cryptographic security while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive theoretical and experimental analyses demonstrate that the proposed encryption system achieves state-of-the-art performance: encryption execution time as low as $2.45 \times 10^{-5}$ seconds, decryption time of $4.47 \times 10^{-5}$ seconds, and an integrity check time of $5.30 \times 10^{-5}$ seconds. Moreover, the ciphertext size is reduced to only 1330 bits while maintaining a 256 -bit security level, representing a significant reduction in storage requirements compared to conventional lattice-based approaches. These results confirm that our scheme not only provides strong quantum-resistant security guarantees but also delivers excellent efficiency and scalability, making it a viable candidate for secure communications in bandwidth-limited and resource-constrained environments in the quantum era.

We examine key use cases such as Peer-to-Peer (P2P) energy trading, microgrid management, and Electric Vehicle (EV) charging, emphasizing how smart contracts automate transactions and enhance security. The report also discusses significant technical, regulatory, economic, and social challenges hindering widespread adoption, including scalability, interoperability, privacy, and evolving regulatory frameworks. Finally, it explores future trends such as advanced cryptographic techniques, blockchain-based cloud infrastructure, and postquantum algorithms, underscoring the imperative for sustained research and development to realize a decentralized, efficient, and sustainable energy future.

venue: 2025 9th International Conference on Cryptography, Security and Privacy (CSP)
title: Further Attacks on the Micali-Schnorr Pseudorandom Generator
abstract: The Micali-Schnorr pseudorandom generator has been in use since its inception in 1990. However, serious concerns about the possibility of a backdoor have been raised since its security is not tightly coupled to the RSA problem. The main contributions include: extending the state of the art in small state attacks by uncovering a new range of vulnerable parameter choices, with accompanying implementation that proves practical and theoretical viability of the extended attack; existence of vulnerable exponents, with an algorithm to generate such exponents for any moduli; development of a framework to using only an exponent's public moduli to detect backdoors and malicious constructions. The main implications of our findings are practical attacks towards non-standard implementations and progress towards a full break; we thus need to be vigilant around niche and inadvertent usage of such a generator.

title: Quantum Artificial Intelligence for Critical Infrastructure: A Survey and Vision
abstract: Critical infrastructures (CI)-including power grids, financial systems, communication networks, and transportation networks-are essential to societal stability and economic security. As these systems grow increasingly complex and interconnected, they face mounting challenges in scalability, robustness, real-time decision-making, and data privacy. While classical artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques have been applied to enhance CI monitoring, optimization, and control, they are often constrained by data heterogeneity, centralized architectures, and limited adaptability. Quantum computing (QC), known for its potential to solve certain computational problems exponentially faster than classical methods, has opened new possibilities in this domain. Quantum artificial intelligence (QAI), which combines quantum computing with AI techniques, offers transformative opportunities, particularly through paradigms such as federated quantum machine learning (FedQML) and quantum reinforcement learning (QRL). These approaches promise privacy-preserving distributed intelligence and dynamic control across CI systems. In this article, we survey recent developments in QAI and explore their applications in critical infrastructure domains. We also highlight key challenges and outline a forward-looking roadmap toward resilient, secure, and quantum-enhanced infrastructure systems.

venue: 2025 57th North American Power Symposium (NAPS)
title: Decentralized Federated Learning for Distributed Energy Resources and Networks
abstract: Distributed Energy Resources (DER) and related assets, such as solar photovoltaics (PV), energy storage systems (ESS), and electric vehicles (EVs), generate large volumes of sensitive operational data that challenge traditional centralized machine learning (ML) approaches due to privacy, bandwidth, and scalability concerns. This paper reviews federated learning (FL) as a decentralized solution that keeps data local while collaboratively training models across DER assets. We compare a range of key FL algorithms, examining their ability to handle non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data, fairness, robustness, and communication efficiency. The review also covers various FL architectures, including serverless frameworks that demonstrate notable performance improvements. We highlight practical FL applications in DERs, including anomaly detection and load forecasting, and discuss real-world challenges such as data heterogeneity, security vulnerabilities, and communication bottlenecks.

venue: 2025 IEEE First International Conference on Innovations in Engineering and Next-Generation Technologies for Sustainability (ICINVENTS)
title: A Review of AWS IoT: Architecture, Applications, and Research Directions
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) has emerged as one of the most transformative paradigms in modern computing, enabling billions of connected devices to sense, process, and transmit data. This growth poses challenges in scalability, security, and real-time data management. Cloud platforms, particularly Amazon Web Services (AWS), have become central enablers of large-scale IoT deployments due to their comprehensive service ecosystem. This paper presents a review of AWS IoT, focusing on its architecture, applications, and open research directions. We analyze core components such as AWS IoT Core, Lambda, Greengrass, and data services, highlighting their roles in enabling cloud-edge integration and secure device management. A survey of academic literature and industrial case studies demonstrates AWS IoT's practical adoption across healthcare, agriculture, and smart city domains. Comparative analysis with Microsoft Azure IoT and Google Cloud IoT positions AWS as a scalable and secure platform, while identifying limitations in latency, cost, and provisioning complexity. Finally, we outline future research opportunities in federated learning, energy-efficient edge inference, protocol interoperability, and blockchain-based provisioning. This review provides a consolidated reference for researchers and practitioners aiming to leverage AWS IoT for next-generation intelligent systems.

venue: 2025 5th International Conference on Mobile Networks and Wireless Communications (ICMNWC)
title: Empirical Research on Intelligent Energy Management in PV-EV Integrated Smart Grids using Machine Learning and Deep Learning-Based Optimization Approaches
abstract: In recent times, effective energy management in power systems with photovoltaic resources and Electric Vehicle (EV) storage increasingly requires maximizing efficiency, reliability, and sustainability. The issue of solar intermittency combined with the variability of EV charging and discharging challenges requires intelligent adaptive control strategies. Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods including machine learning applied to forecasting, optimal scheduling, and near real-time optimization of energy management provide the ability to optimize in real-time utilization of renewables, support energy throughput management, mitigate peak load, perform direct load control, and engage in or off-load EV battery storage resources as part of the Vehicle-To-Grid (V2G) power exchange. The established benefits of employing AI technologies in smart grids with PV and EV storage come with challenges such as data heterogeneity and diversity, model interpretability, scalability to changes in use, and deployment on real-time basis. This survey discusses recent algorithms based on AI techniques applied to smart grids with PV and EV storage providing value to predictive control and other multi-optimization objectives. Future directions include how hybrid AI models are developed to support resilient, privacy-preserving, and interoperable energy management strategies for next-generation smart grid.

title: Big Data, Cloud Computing, and Internet-Enabled Infrastructures for Sustainable Development
abstract: Sustainability has become a major global concern and this necessitates the need to develop novel methods to handle the environmental, social, and economic resources in an effective manner. The combination of Big Data, cloud computing and the infrastructures enabled by the Internet provides the unprecedented opportunities to facilitate the process of sustainable development due to the real time monitoring, data-based decision making, and intelligent resource optimization. Big Data analytics and cloud computing allow the extraction of actionable insights out of very large and heterogeneous datasets that have been gathered through IoT devices and sensors and, at the same time, offer scalable, flexible, and power-efficient platforms to process and store the data. Internet-connected infrastructures such as edge and fog computing support low latency, real time control of systems that are critical to environmental management, smart cities and industrial processes. New technologies like analytics powered by AI, blockchain to manage resources in a transparent way, green cloud computing, and digital twins will also increase the efficiency, robustness, and responsibility of sustainable systems. Nonetheless, bumps on the road, including excessive energy usage, interoperability, data privacy, and adoption limitations in developing nations, still exist, however, research and innovation are ongoing to create intelligent, adaptive, and equitable solutions. This survey provides a broad picture of the principles, usage, upcoming trends, challenges, and future study directions, and states the revolutionary potential of these technologies in realizing the sustainable development objectives.

venue: 2025 4th International Conference on Embedded Systems and Artificial Intelligence (ESAI)
title: A Unified Security Framework for Smart City AI-Systems: Cross-Domain Vulnerability Analysis and Mitigation Strategies
abstract: The rapid proliferation of AI-driven systems across smart city infrastructure has created a complex landscape of interconnected security vulnerabilities that transcend traditional domain boundaries. While existing research predominantly focuses on single domain security analysis, this paper presents the first comprehensive cross-domain security framework for smart city AI-implementations. We synthesize insights from cyber security research across traffic management, energy grids, healthcare, and public safety to identify five critical vulnerability categories: data centric attacks (poisoning and integrity violations), model centric attacks (adversarial examples and evasion), infrastructure compromises (supply chain and edge computing), operational integrity threats (bias and concept drift), and privacy violations (inference and reconstruction attacks). In this paper, we do two main things. First, we build a unified vulnerability taxonomy that organizes threats by how the attack happens, which part of the city it affects, and how the effects can spread. This shows security gaps that don’t appear when each system is analyzed on its own. Second, we propose a mitigation road map that ranks countermeasures by how feasible they are, what they cost in terms of resources, and how much disruption they could cause in the city. Our risk matrix highlights data poisoning and algorithmic bias as the top priorities (risk scores 4.0 and 3.7). We also show that, if the prioritized mitigations are applied, overall vulnerability exposure can be reduced by roughly $\mathbf{5 0 - 7 5 \%}$ over a 12-18 month period.

venue: 2025 IEEE International Workshop on Metrology for Living Environment (MetroLivEnv)
title: Intelligent Coordination System for Autonomous Domestic Heating: An AI-Driven Test-Bench
abstract: The integration of renewable energy sources and smart technologies in domestic heating systems has become a critical focus in recent years. However, the complex landscape of competing technologies and need-to-comply normative requirements presents significant challenges for practitioners and endusers. In this paper, we first review the principal state-of-theart technologies commonly employed in the industry. We then analyze the key normative requirements for implementing such systems in real-world scenarios. Based on this comprehensive review, we design a smart energy coordination system tailored for domestic buildings according to state-of-the-art practices, which will serve as a baseline for evaluating and comparing other novel, competing solutions. This testbed provides a common ground for assessing the effectiveness and compliance of various energy management strategies, ensuring they meet both technical and regulatory standards. To validate our approach, we implemented the proposed solution on a real-world residential testbed. Our work contributes to the development of reliable, efficient, and adaptable smart energy systems, supporting the transition towards renewable energy solutions and sustainable home automation.

venue: 2025 2nd International Conference on Computational Intelligence and Computing Applications (ICCICA)
title: Exploring AI-Driven Approaches for Predicting Electric Vehicle Charging Behaviour: A Literature Review
abstract: The demand for intelligent systems that can accurately forecast the charging behavior and demand of electric vehicles (EVs) has increased due to the world's rapid transition to electric mobility. Planning infrastructure, maximizing energy distribution, and raising user satisfaction all depend on an understanding of charging trends. In order to predict EV charging behavior, this study provides a thorough analysis of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven methodologies. Linear regression, decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, XGBoost, and neural networks are just a few of the supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning techniques that are analyzed in this study in order to assess their predictive capabilities and limitations across a range of datasets. With information on environmental factors, charging infrastructure, and socioeconomic profiles, these datasets offer a comprehensive picture of the variables affecting EV user behavior. The results show that deep learning and ensemble algorithms, especially Gradient Boosting frameworks and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) algorithms, provide better performance in capturing temporal variations in charging demand and nonlinear dependencies. Additionally, there are chances for dynamic energy management, lower grid load, and fair energy distribution when AI-based predictive models are integrated with smart grids and Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) systems. Nonetheless, the study points out issues with privacy protection, real-time adaptability, model interpretability, and data scarcity. Prediction accuracy and scalability can be greatly improved by addressing these problems with hybrid models, federated learning, and sophisticated optimization techniques. In the end, this review emphasizes how AI-driven predictive modelling is essential to creating intelligent, user-centred, and sustainable EV ecosystems, which in turn supports international initiatives to create cleaner and more effective transportation systems.

title: Blockchain Based IoT Security: A Comprehensive Review of Architectures Challenges and Future Directions
abstract: Healthcare, transportation, and smart cities marked revolutionary growth in the market. They are increasingly relying on the Internet of Things (IoT) that may be appropriately identified with strong privacy and security threats. The decentralized, scalable function of IoT devices leaves them uniquely at risk of cyberattacks or breaches. Many security schemes depend on centralized approaches that just don’t fit in this scenario. A technology like blockchain addresses existing security concerns by facilitating automation using smart contracts and secure communication. This article offers a coherent and thoughtful exposition on the growing security threats to IoT. It addresses gaps in IoT architecture and configuration within pseudo-omnichannels. The discussion further emphasizes latency, energy efficiency of connected devices, and the costs tied to rigid cyber infrastructures that may fall short. The impacts of security are examined using frameworks dependent on artificial intelligence, lightweight blockchains, and post-quantum cryptography as a basis of secure omnichannel architecture. Additionally, the framework addresses universal receipt control and gate access mechanisms as include parts of IoT security.

abstract: This paper reviews the role of the Internet of Things (IoT) in developing smart homes, smart cities, and eHealth systems, focusing on how information and communication technologies (ICT) enhance quality of life. title: DigiRES: Digital Integration of Multi-Energy Flexibility Assets in Regional Energy Systems
abstract: The ongoing energy transition, driven by the proliferation of distributed renewable energy sources (DRES), necessitates advanced coordination of flexible resources across multiple energy carriers. This paper investigates recent developments and challenges in enabling multi-energy flexibility within regional energy systems, emphasizing the integration of electricity, heating, cooling, and transportation vectors. We analyze the emerging paradigm of Flexibility-as-a-Service (FaaS), which aims to unlock and aggregate flexibility from distributed assets via innovative business models and intelligent digital platforms. Building on this foundation, we introduce a conceptual framework developed in the DigiRES project, which leverages semi/self-learning AI models, an Internet-of-Energy (IoE) platform, and structured market layers to optimize flexibility allocation in a secure and privacy-preserving manner. Through a comprehensive review of enabling technologies, regulatory and market barriers, and validation across demonstration sites in the Netherlands, Sweden, and Belgium, this paper highlights the key opportunities and practical constraints for realizing scalable, interoperable, and regionally adaptable multi-energy flexibility markets.

title: Distributed Reinforcement Learning for Intelligent Decision-Making
abstract: Distributed Reinforcement Learning (DRL), as a cutting-edge method in intelligent decision-making, demonstrates significant potential in smart grids, autonomous driving, and intelligent unmanned systems owing to its decentralized architecture, efficient multi-agent coordination capability, and adaptability to complex dynamic environments. This paper systematically reviews the theoretical framework of DRL and its advancements in these domains. In smart grids, DRL effectively addresses the volatility challenges induced by highpenetration distributed energy resources (DERs) through modelfree optimization, substantially enhancing dynamic scheduling and real-time decision-making performance. For autonomous driving, the graph neural network-enhanced DRL framework resolves multimodal perception-decision fusion challenges, with simulations verifying its superior performance over conventional rule-based methods in complex traffic scenarios. Furthermore, DRL exhibits remarkable scalability in multi-agent cooperative control and autonomous decision-making for intelligent unmanned systems. This paper further analyzes critical challenges in current DRL applications, including communication efficiency, algorithmic scalability, and privacy protection, while proposing future research directions to advance DRL implementations in complex intelligent systems.

abstract: This study examines how Artificial Intelligence (AI) and gamification can promote energy conservation by enhancing consumer engagement and encouraging sustainable behaviors. title: Compliance-by-Design for IoT Cloud Platforms: A Reference Architecture and Case Study
abstract: As IoT ecosystems increasingly rely on cloud platforms to store, process, and manage sensitive data, ensuring compliance with evolving privacy and security regulations has become critical. This paper presents a novel compliance-by-design reference architecture for IoT cloud platforms, which embeds regulatory controls into the system’s operational fabric from the outset. Unlike traditional post-hoc audit models, our approach integrates consent tracking, data retention enforcement, access control, and audit logging as modular, enforceable services across device, gateway, and cloud layers. We validate the architecture through a smart energy monitoring case study, demonstrating high compliance enforcement accuracy, audit readiness, and scalability. Comparative evaluation against state-of-the-art compliance frameworks highlights significant improvements in policy enforcement and latency overhead. The proposed architecture offers a practical and extensible blueprint for building regulationready IoT systems.

title: Accelerating the take-up of LEVs in emerging markets. Findings from Southeast Asia
abstract: Motorised light vehicles, particularly two- and three-wheelers, play a crucial role in mobility and urban logistics across emerging economies, especially in Southeast Asia. While these vehicles offer resource-efficient transportation, their reliance on fossil fuels contributes significantly to air and noise pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. Electrification of these fleets presents a viable pathway to sustainable mobility. Despite growing attention to electric cars, Light Electric Vehicles (LEVs) remain underrepresented in policy and investment strategies in the region. This paper uses a socio-technical transition framework to analyse barriers to LEV adoption and proposes strategic action areas to accelerate their uptake. Key challenges include high upfront costs, limited charging infrastructure, lack of standardisation, and fragmented regulatory frameworks. The study draws on empirical data from surveys, interviews, and regional stakeholder engagements conducted during the development of ASEAN Guidelines on LEVs. It identifies five critical action areas: standardisation, financial and non-financial incentives, stakeholder collaboration, strategic policy frameworks, and incorporation of monitoring and evaluation measures. The findings underscore the need for coordinated public-private efforts, harmonised standards, and time-bound policy targets to unlock the environmental, social, and economic benefits of LEV adoption in Southeast Asia.

venue: 2025 15th IEEE International Conference on Pattern Recognition Systems (ICPRS)
title: Energy Disaggregation Using Radial Basis Function Neural Networks based on Deep Co Training Architecture
abstract: Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM) has emerged as a critical tool in energy management, offering a non- invasive means to disaggregate a building’s total electricity usage into appliance-level consumption. However, existing NILM approaches often require large labeled datasets, raising significant challenges in terms of dataset availability, privacy exposure, and computational burdens. This paper proposes a semi-supervised energy disaggregation approach using a Radial Basis Function Neural Network (RBFNN) within a Deep Co-Training framework. RBFNN’s fast convergence and robustness to noise address key practical issues in NILM research, such as limited labeling and the complexity of real-world power signals. Meanwhile, the co-training paradigm allows two neural networks to iteratively exchange pseudo-labels on unlabeled data, thus significantly reducing the need for extensive ground-truth annotations. We validate our approach on two public datasets, REDD and UK-DALE, disaggregating six household appliances. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance with improved Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score when compared with three state-of-the- art semi-supervised NILM methods. Our work underscores the utility of combining RBFNNs with deep co-training to address data scarcity, computational efficiency, and privacy concerns, ultimately facilitating broader deployment of NILM solutions for energy conservation and sustainability.

venue: 2025 IEEE 13th Region 10 Humanitarian Technology Conference (R10-HTC)
title: Edge-AI Technologies for Sustainability: A Comparative Analysis
abstract: Edge-AI offers a promising strategy for implementing distributed sustainable digital systems by offloading computational tasks from centralized cloud-AI infrastructures to local and energy-efficient devices. This study investigates the potential of edge-AI in key domains for sustainability, including smart energy systems, precision agriculture, sustainable smart cities, industrial IoT, and environmental monitoring. Through a literature review, comparative analysis, and evaluation of practical implementations, this research demonstrates that decentralized inference enables substantial sustainabilityrelated gains. Specifically, edge-AI technologies have shown energy savings of up to 28%, latency reductions of 35%, and bandwidth reductions of up to 60% compared to cloud-based models. These improvements are complemented by improved data privacy through on-device processing and reduced reliance on remote servers. Despite these advantages, challenges such as limited hardware capacity, scalability constraints, integration complexity, and lifecycle concerns persist. This study highlights the critical role of edge-AI technologies in promoting green standards to achieve the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs) by 2030.

venue: 2025 International Conference on Computational Engineering, Sensing Technology and Management (ICCETM)
title: AI-Enabled Strategies For Future-Enterprises: Interfacing Legal Management Practices, And Engineering Systems
abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) strategies represents a paradigm shift in how enterprises achieve sustainability, compliance, and innovation. Future-ready enterprises face increasing pressure from regulators, investors, and society to demonstrate responsible business practices while maintaining competitiveness in rapidly evolving markets. AI-enabled ESG strategies bridge legal frameworks, management practices, and engineering systems by offering real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and automated decision support. These systems not only enhance regulatory compliance but also optimize energy efficiency, supply chain transparency, and risk management. From automated carbon tracking to AI-driven social impact assessments, enterprises are leveraging data intelligence to align corporate objectives with sustainable outcomes. However, challenges such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, and fragmented global ESG regulations remain significant hurdles. This paper explores the multidisciplinary dimensions of AI in ESG by examining its interplay with law, management, and engineering. Through critical review and methodological design, it highlights how AI-enabled ESG strategies can build resilient, ethical, and future-ready enterprises. The study contributes to a growing body of knowledge by offering a holistic framework that unites legal obligations, managerial innovations, and technological infrastructures for sustainability-driven transformation. venue: 2025 International Conference on Technology and Policy in Energy and Electric Power (ICT-PEP)
title: Designing a Sustainable Power Distribution System for Industrial Growth: A Case Study of Grand Batang City
abstract: The Grand Batang City Industrial Estate is growing quickly, with energy use rising by 900% in just one year. This means that the electrical distribution system needs to be reliable and adaptable. The goal of this study is to improve the current distribution network and come up with the best system structure to meet future electricity needs. Using ETAP software for load profile analysis, demand forecasting, and technical simulations, a spindle structure with three connected substations was chosen as the best option. The results of the study show that improvements to network configuration must be made on a regular basis and in line with changing industrial load forecasts. The development plan includes changing the system in 2025, adding more capacity to the transformers in 2026, and adding new substation in 2030. These suggestions improve privacy and the ability to keep things going while also providing a framework for a long-lasting electrical system that can be used in other industries.

venue: 2025 25th Conference of the Electric Power Supply Industry (CEPSI)
title: Toward Seamless IoT Interoperability for Energy and Mobility Integration: A Systemic Perspective
abstract: The convergence of energy and mobility systems, accelerated by electric vehicle adoption and the rise of smart grids, presents significant challenges and opportunities for system interoperability. This paper investigates how Internet of Things (IoT) technologies can enable seamless integration across these domains by addressing technical, semantic, and regulatory barriers. We identify key challenges such as legacy infrastructure, protocol fragmentation, data heterogeneity, and institutional misalignment. To address these, we review enabling solutions including IoT middleware platforms, ontology-driven data models, standardized communication protocols, and privacy-preserving frameworks. A layered architecture is presented to illustrate how modular and scalable integration can be achieved in real-world systems. Additionally, we highlight emerging research opportunities in adaptive architectures, decentralized data governance, semantic automation, and secure edge intelligence. By synthesizing multidisciplinary insights, this work provides a foundation for developing resilient and interoperable energy-mobility ecosystems, supporting the broader goals of sustainability, decarbonization, and digital transformation.

title: Communication Technologies for Smart Cities: Enabling Connectivity, Efficiency, and Urban Intelligence
abstract: The high rate of urbanization in cities across the globe has demanded the creation of smart infrastructures that would make use of advanced communication technologies to improve efficiency, sustainability, and services to the citizens. This survey gives an in-depth description of both wired and wireless communication systems, such as fiber optics, Ethernet, cellular (4G/5G/6G), Wi-Fi, LPWAN, and satellite-based networks and how they can be used to facilitate seamless communications to diverse smart city applications. The upcoming technologies of Software-Defined Networking (SDN), Network Function Virtualization (NFV), edge and fog computing, visible light communication (VLC) and future 6G networks are addressed in relation to their scalability, flexibility and low-latency communication. The smart transportation, healthcare, energy control, public safety, environmental monitoring, and intelligent buildings are the main examples of key applications that show how much communication networks can change the urban ecosystem. The survey also includes issues concerning security, privacy, interoperability, energy efficiency, and cost of deployment and gives an insight on the drawbacks of the existing infrastructures. Lastly, the potential research areas including AI based network management, blockchain based secure communication, integration of IoT-edge-cloud framework, and quantum communication are discussed to inform the creation of robust, secure, and highly efficient networks. The purpose of this work is to enlighten the researchers, policymakers, and urban planners on how to develop smart cities of the new generation.

venue: 2025 IEEE/ACIS 29th International Conference on Software Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, Networking and Parallel/Distributed Computing (SNPD)
title: Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading in a Local Energy Market Using Quantum Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Recent years have witnessed a significant transformation in the sources of energy and its distribution among consumers and prosumers. Renewable energy sources (RES) such as photovoltaic have become particularly popular. However, RES requires a new approach to manage energy demand and supply by leveraging distributed energy generation. In this context, a useful paradigm is a peer-to-peer (P2P) energy marketplace, which is a trading mechanism that actively involves consumers and prosumers in trading electricity using state-of-the-art information and communication technologies. Accordingly, we focus on optimizing total energy trading costs by using quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) to ensure that local generation is first consumed by energy consumers within a local community. This is followed by a proposal of blockchain-based energy trading systems to facilitate decentralized, secured, and privacy-protected trading platforms for the trading participants. To this end, we use three optimization techniques - linear optimization techniques, reinforcement learning, and QRL - and analyze their performance. Simulation results show that the agents learning using quantum computing converge faster than those of the other two optimization techniques.

venue: 2025 3rd International Conference on Cyber Resilience (ICCR)
title: Quantum Cryptography for Smart Grid Cyber-Physical Systems: A Comparative Review
abstract: The recent advancement of smart grid systems, integrating cyber-physical systems with information and communication technologies enables real-time monitoring, control, and data transmission. However, these operations often inherently insecure communication infrastructures increasing exposure to cyber threats and data breaches. Consequently, cryptographic authenticated and key agreement protocols address cyber-attacks, threats, and vulnerabilities to protect data privacy and security in smart grid. Meanwhile, quantum computing progression is rapidly footprinted in real-world application thus quantum computing-based Grover's and Shor’s algorithm is capable for breaking classical cryptographic algorithms mathematical advances. Therefore, this review explores the adaptability of quantum computing, examines its impact on classical cryptography vulnerabilities, and highlights the role of quantum cryptography in enhancing security and scalability of smart grid cyber-physical systems. Accordingly, a comparative analysis was conducted to assess the security and performance of Rivest-Shamir Adleman, elliptic curve cryptography and digital signature algorithms against quantum cryptography for highlighting their respective strengths and limitations in quantum era context. This review provides a foundation of future researchers for integrate quantum technology and develop quantum-resilient solutions that overcome the constraints of classical cryptography.

venue: IEEE Transactions on Sustainable Computing
title: Semantic Communication-Based Low-Carbon Sustainable Framework for Person Re-Identification
abstract: Person re-identification (Re-ID) is a critical technology in security systems and video surveillance. However, most of the existing methods focused on precise Re-ID, which not only neglect the transmission overheads, computing energy consumption and carbon emissions, but are unsustainable. Furthermore, the personal semantics is usually blurred and distorted in real-world scenarios due to the bird’s eye view (BEV) of cameras. Cross-illumination and face-coverings also weakened the key personal semantics. Such deficiencies have resulted in a substantial amount of carbon emissions and poor Re-ID performance. To reduce the video transmission overheads, computing energy consumption and carbon emissions yet guaranteeing the accuracy of Re-ID, this paper proposes a novel semantic communication-based low-carbon sustainable framework (SC-LCSF) for Re-ID. SC-LCSF adopts the semantic encoder based on an enhanced semantics-aware attention mechanism (ESA-SE) to extract the personal semantics. Only semantic information is transmitted at the semantic layer, which is then decoded into personal IDs by the multi-granularity semantic decoder (MG-SD). Two widely used public datasets, Market-1501 and CUHK03, and a newly curated real-world dataset, HZAU-SCUEC01, are used to train SC-LCSF and to evaluate its performance. Experimental results show that compared to the state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, SC-LCSF achieves the best Rank-1 and mAP accuracy on all the datasets. Furthermore, SC-LCSF has a significant performance enhancement in low-carbon sustainable computing – the transmission data amount, CPU power consumption, CPU temperature, GPU power consumption, GPU temperature and Re-ID delay have a reduction of 96.8%, 39.6%, 27.9%, 40.9%, 29.7%, and 76.6%, respectively.

title: A Real-Time Implementation and Validation of Federated Learning for Grid Services
abstract: Grid-edge devices are becoming increasingly important in the energy transition. Preserving privacy was not previously considered an important aspect for power grid operations, but with the increased proliferation of customer-owned assets, it is now an essential consideration. Several mechanisms have been proposed to provide privacy for non-utility owned assets in the power grid. Federated learning (FL) is one method gaining prominence in this area. Although FL has been used for other applications, such as auto-complete in phones, there has not been much investigation into whether these approaches are feasible for grid applications. In this work, we use a research platform with real-time simulators and hardware-in-the-loop capabilities to investigate how FL can be applied to grid-edge devices, and we present the potential grid services that can be derived for these devices. We discuss the computational challenges with deploying complex FL approaches, and we explore several grid services, including participation in retail electricity markets, voltage control, and resilience-driven reconfiguration.

title: Survey on Privacy-Aware Federated Learning Frameworks for Energy Systems within Smart Grids
abstract: The global transition towards Smart Grids (SGs) has brought about significant advancements in energy management and efficiency. To sustain these advancements, robust data-driven models trained on large-scale energy datasets are essential. However, the bidirectional flow of data and increasing connectivity within SG infrastructures have introduced cybersecurity and privacy vulnerabilities, raising concerns about the protection of sensitive consumer and operational information as well as regulatory compliance. Federated Learning (FL), a decentralized machine learning paradigm, has emerged as a promising solution to these challenges, enabling models to be trained at the edge while ensuring the accuracy of a global model. Although numerous studies have explored the application of FL in the Internet of Things (IoT), this paper presents a survey of most recent and impactful literature on the application of FL algorithms within the SG domain. Our analysis integrates findings from key studies, categorizing the primary applications of FL to address common challenges such as communication overhead and statistical heterogeneity arising from non-independently and identically distributed (non-IID) data. We also explore promising avenues for future research in FL and anomaly detection. Furthermore, we examine various FL architectures, threat models, privacy-preserving mechanisms, and the gaps in existing datasets and protocols.

title: Adoption of Smart Energy Management Applications for Smart Grids: Roles of Trust, Data Transparency, and Perceived Usefulness
abstract: Smart energy management applications have become a significant user facing service component of smart grid services, though they are yet to be adopted across users and platforms. The paper examines the motivators of Adoption Intention on smart energy management applications with the concentration on five main user perceptions pertaining to value, credibility, and service experience. The survey data were obtained from 103 participants who had previously used energy management and electricity service application. The study applies linear regression to estimate the effects of System Trust, Data Transparency, Usefulness, Security and Privacy, and Ease of Use on Adoption Intention. The results indicate that Usefulness is the strongest positive predictor of adoption intention, while System Trust and Data Transparency also have significant positive effects. Security and Privacy is positive and non-significant and Ease of Use has a marginal positive effect. The results imply that the perceived practical value and trust in the general service system are the main determinants of adoption in the context of supported by the practice of transparent data. The implications are related to the utilities and service providers interested in enhancing the uptake of the users through better value focused feature design, trust establishment, and more explicit communication of data.

venue: 2026 11th International Conference on Smart and Sustainable Technologies (SpliTech)
title: What Data Do You Really Need? Feature-Level Privacy Analysis for Household Energy Forecasting
abstract: Accurate household energy forecasting benefits from granular smart meter data, yet the EU General Data Protection Regulation demands data minimization. Existing privacypreserving approaches (differential privacy, federated learning) protect data after collection. We ask a complementary question: which feature categories can be removed entirely before collection? We propose a feature-level privacy analysis that organizes forecasting inputs into four privacy levels, from highly invasive appliance-level activity traces to publicly available metadata. Through evaluation across three household energy datasets (Canada, France, United Kingdom), representing basic metering, circuit-level monitoring, and fully instrumented smart homes, we quantify the forecasting cost of progressively removing private data. Our results show that per-appliance traces and activity labels are removable at near-zero accuracy cost (0-3%), while energy-derived features frequently categorized as “behavioral” carry 17-19 percentage points of predictive value and leak consumption patterns equivalent to raw energy data. A standard hourly smart meter with building metadata provides near-optimal forecasting. Sub-metering hardware is not justified by accuracy gains. At the strictest privacy level, only datasets with building metadata (occupancy, house size) outperform a persistence baseline. Under the recommended collection policy, new household predictions stabilize within 6 hours of meter deployment. All findings replicate under Ridge regression, confirming model independence. These results provide empirical guidance for GDPR-compliant data minimization in smart meter infrastructure.

title: Opportunities, Characteristics and Challenges of Smart Grids
abstract: Future electricity should be flexible, accessible, reliable and economically viable for them to achieve the smart grid initiative which include the reduction in greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) through increased penetration of Renewable Energy Sources (RES) such as solar, wind and other micro-sources. The grid is undergoing significant changes because of increasing demand of electricity, growing political pressure and public awareness on the need to reduce carbon emission and integrate large scale renewable power by blending information and communication technologies with power system operation which led to the microgrid concept which has evolved into smart grid technologies. Smart grids constitute an evolution of traditional grids by integrating digital communication, automation, and data analytics in the conventional grids. The smart grids offer improved efficiency and more efficient renewable integration enhanced by the two-way communication and self-healing ability. However, they face significant technical, non-technical and economic hurdles like high cots, cybersecurity risks, interoperability, privacy and confidentiality issues. Smart grids are networks employing digital communications, automated controls, and advanced sensors for optimal power generation, distribution, and use by offering efficiency, sustainability, and reliability. The conventional power grids are experiencing significant expansion which calls for reliability and efficiency in operation and maintenance to guarantee efficient and sustainable power generation, delivery and end use capable of supporting a diverse, heterogeneous operating measures and devices like smart appliances, smart meters, and renewable plug-in vehicles, energy resources generation systems supported by the grid. The growing electricity demand, expansion of the grid and high number of generating plants and customers have continuously increased the complexity and challenges of the electricity grid in delivering quality and reliable electricity to end users. These challenges require greater system reliability, improved efficiency, more security, cleaner environment and higher system sustainability can be realized by using smarter electricity grids. The smart grid is a rapidly growing concept in the electricity industry that has potential to transform the use of variable renewables variable loads and improve energy efficiency in grid power systems. The smart grid technologies have demonstrated potential to revolutionize the electricity grid by means of two-way communications to improve power system reliability, economy, efficiency, and sustainability in power generation, transmission, and distribution. title: FedShield-DERMS: Federated Intrusion Detection for Smart Grids
abstract: The rapid shift to utilizing distributed energy resources (DER) in Distributed Energy Resource Management Systems (DERMS) has been accompanied by a number of cybersecurity challenges for modern smart grids. These challenges include injection of false data and denial of service attacks, as well as a number of other, more subtle, reconnaissance-based attacks. Most of the existing research in the area of intrusion detection has relied either on the collection of data at a centralized location or extensive privacy assumptions, while much of the data is composed of independent, identically distributed data. These assumptions and methodologies do not capture the interest of the highly heterogeneous smart grids. This paper reviews federated learning-based intrusion detection published between 2022 and 2026, and analyzes the proliferation of non-robust, inefficient, and adversarial frameworks with no knowledge of the DERMS communication protocols. With the goal of minimizing these gaps, we present FedShield-DERMS. FedShield-DERMS is a federated intrusion detection system composed of a lightweight, hybrid CNN-LSTM local model framework, a trust-weighted secure aggregation approach, and differential-privacy noise tailored to cover the DERMS. A controlled evaluation framework for the federated intrusion detection system is proposed to assess detection, and intrusion metrics, including communication overhead, in comparison to centralized and conventional federated approaches.

venue: 2026 3rd International Conference on Connected Innovation and Technology (ICCITX)
title: Federated Learning Attacks in Smart Grid Energy Forecasting: Threat Model, Comparative Analysis, and Impact Mapping
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is increasingly adopted in Smart Grids to support privacy-preserving analytics across multiple stakeholders, notably for short-horizon energy forecasting such as load, PV generation, and net-load prediction. However, FL introduces a distinct attack surface through the exchange of model updates, and adversarial manipulations can propagate into operational decision errors. This paper studies the impact of major FL threat families in the specific context of Smart Grid forecasting, with an emphasis on how Smart Grid constraints (heterogeneity, non-IID data, drift, and time-critical operation) shape attack feasibility, stealth, and consequences. We first define a unified and realistic threat model for forecasting deployments. We then provide a contextualized taxonomy covering data poisoning, model poisoning, backdoor, and inference attacks, and propose a compact qualitative comparison along availability/resilience, integrity, confidentiality/privacy, and detectability. Building on this analysis, we establish an impact mapping that links machine learning (ML) failure modes (degradation, bias, trigger-conditioned errors, or leakage) to operational risks in forecasting-driven grid functions. Finally, we outline a lightweight reference framework to guide future experimental evaluations and the design of protection mechanisms for Smart Grid forecasting.

venue: 2026 Intermountain Engineering, Technology and Computing (IETC)
title: Cyberattack Detection in Smart Grids: A Survey of Machine Learning Approaches and Challenges
abstract: Smart Grids utilize bidirectional energy and data flows enabled by Information and Communications Technology (ICT) to create significant vulnerabilities to cyberattacks that affect grid reliability, economic performance, and public safety. Machine Learning approaches have shown potential to support intrusion detection systems; however, prior studies lack systematic comparisons across attack vectors and analyses of the deployment trade-offs associated with smart grid cybersecurity methods. By comparing various architectures across attack types, results indicate that model selection should be topology-aware. For example, Graph Neural Networks showed superior performance in detecting false data injection attacks by encoding the physical structure of the power grid, while Transformer-based models excelled in detecting electricity theft attacks by capturing long-range temporal dependencies in historical electricity consumption data. Additionally, privacy-preserving federated learning demonstrated reasonable accuracy for binary classification problems, but it has limited capability for multi-class classification, and adversarial robustness remains severely underexplored, with fewer than 7% of reviewed works testing for evasion attacks. Dataset concentration represents a major obstacle to generalizing results: nearly all false data injection literature uses IEEE synthetic systems, while theft detection relies on a single benchmark. The findings provide practitioners with evidence-based guidance for selecting architectures and researchers with a roadmap that addresses robustness, explainability, and real-world validation.

venue: 2026 6th International Conference on Electrical, Computer and Energy Technologies (ICECET)
title: Review of Privacy and Security Mechanisms in Smart Cities: From Data Protection to Threat Prevention
abstract: Privacy and cybersecurity systems in smart cities are critically reviewed and assessed in the present paper by synthesizing 21 peer-reviewed publications, published between 2018 and 2024, but the works on the topic published prior to 2018 are also acknowledged to provide background information. The paper not only classifies these mechanisms, but further compares them against the frameworks of privacy protection, scalability, governance and resilience, a separation between the technical and legal approaches. The systematic literature review was conducted based on the five-phase protocol presented by Kitchenham with the assistance of a PRISMAlike quality assessment of the studies included. These mechanisms were categorized into five themes that comprise blockchain-based architectures, intrusion detection and machine learning models, privacy-preserving learning systems, legal and governance frameworks and hybrid trust-based architectures. An evaluation lens Technology, Governance, and Resilience (TGR) triad was used to make comparative synthesis and prioritize both performance and limitation and applicability at the city level. As determined in the review, blockchain-enabled schemes dominate in the recent researches and offer immutability, auditability, but have a limitation of latency, interoperability and high power-consumption. Methods of machine learning are more accurate in detection, yet can not be interpreted or adversarial resistant. These regulations such as GDPR are enforced but not dynamic and thus, they lag behind the evolving technologies. Hybrid trust based models are promising to be integrated yet they are computationally expensive. The review has identified ten gaps, which include dynamic consent, adversarial robustness, explainable AI and cross-jurisdictional interoperability. The results indicate that scalable, modular, and legally entrenched structures are immediately required in order to balance privacy, cost, and social trust of urban infrastructures. Practice implications may be reduced costs of cybersecurity breaches, enhanced citizen trust in smart services, and advice to policymakers on how compliance may be incorporated into technical design instead of ex-post regulation. The current research is the only one that combines technological, governance and economical views into a comparative framework. It provides a resilient, privacy-conscious and economically viable roadmap towards co-designing smart city systems by placing post-2018 mechanisms in a broader historical context to guide researchers, practitioners, and policymakers to implement a coherent approach to smarter cities

abstract: The ongoing digital transformation in power grids has made the Internet of Things (IoT) a critical component for the development of next generation smart grids. The article provides a detailed review on technologies related to IoT and their utilization within the current power grid ecosystem that includes various IoT layers like perception layer sensors, advanced metering infrastructure (AMI), and cloud computing/ artificial intelligence(AI) based energy management platforms. The paper discusses the layered IoT architecture for smart grids, explores various wireless communications solutions including ZigBee, LoRaWAN, NB-IoT and 5G. The article also examines enabling IoT technologies including big data analysis, blockchain-based secure transactions for energy trading and federated learning for privacy preservation. Emerging IoT paradigms like blockchain-enabled DL networks, lattice-based cryptography schemes for IoT devices and software-defined vehicular edge computing solutions are analyzed as critical components of next generation secure smart grid infrastructures. Application of IoT in demand response, fault detection, renewable sources integration, and distributed energy resource management is explored systematically. Issues associated with interoperability, scalability, cyberattacks, and real-time latency are also addressed with proposed mitigation approaches. Finally, the paper concludes with future research directions related to integrating AI and IoT technologies in the smart grid ecosystem.

title: A Comprehensive Review on Power Theft Detection Techniques in Electrical Distribution Systems
abstract: Non-Technical Losses (NTLs) from theft, metering errors, and billing irregularities continue to affect distribution utilities by reducing revenue, distorting load measurements, and complicating regulatory compliance. In many jurisdictions, the associated financial impact reaches billions of dollars annually. The deployment of Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) and improved data acquisition systems has expanded the analytical options for electricity theft detection (ETD), leading to techniques ranging from statistical screening and machine learning to deep representation learning, state-estimation-based inference, and privacy-preserving computation. Evaluation is increasingly shaped by deployment factors such as computational cost, privacy exposure, inspection overhead, and regulatory requirements. This review provides a structured overview of current ETD methods and highlights emerging research directions, including federated analytics, DER-aware modelling, adversarial behavior, and zerotrust metering.

venue: 2026 IEEE Texas Power and Energy Conference (TPEC)
title: Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Neural Architecture Search in Federated EVCS Security
abstract: Rapid adoption of Electric Vehicle Charging Stations (EVCS) has generated cybersecurity vulnerabilities in smart grid infrastructure, necessitating new anomaly detection systems that can react to emerging threats and protect data privacy. Federated Learning (FL) keeps data decentralized to protect privacy; however, FedAvg and FedProx use static, homogenous neural architectures that cannot adjust to client heterogeneity or changing attack patterns. Even FL Neural Architecture Search (NAS) approaches generate fixed designs per client without dynamic modification. This study proposes FedRNAS, a new framework that combines reinforcement learning (RL) with neural architecture search to enable dynamic model customization in federated environments. Our approach uses a Q-learning agent to continually update neural architectures for each client based on real-time performance feedback and changing threat scenarios. FedRNAS achieves 96.75% detection accuracy, a notable $+1.31 {\%}$ improvement over standard FedNAS, according to extensive tests conducted on four EVCS datasets from the IEEE-123 bus system. Our work is the first to demonstrate RL-driven dynamic NAS in federated learning, allowing for autonomous adaptation to emerging cybersecurity threats in critical infrastructure while keeping the privacy benefits of federated methods.

title: Cyber Security in Wireless Charging Systems for Electric Vehicles
abstract: Wireless charging technology for electric vehicles (EVs) has attracted rather significant interest because it removes the use of physical connectors, additionally promoting apparent user convenience, efficiency, and user automation within the broader transportation infrastructure system. However, wireless power transfer combined with advances in smart technologies and communication networks presents new challenges in cyber security. With electric vehicle charging systems being connected to the smart grid, integrating with the Internet of Things (IoT), and using cloud-based data storage and management, they become vulnerable to hacker attack vectors, such as eavesdropping, data manipulation, denial-of-service, and energy theft. Cyberattacks on wireless charging could result in more than just disruptions to user charging, having serious implications for user privacy, impacts on grid security and stability, and safety in the transportation system at large. This paper aims to expose the key cyber security concerns wireless charging systems face for EVs, threats and risks, and mitigation. Through a comprehensive literature review, we consider existing research, as well as identify gaps. The proposed methodology considers existing cryptographic protocols, utilize intrusion detection systems frameworks, and suggest blockchain security to promote resilience. Validation through simulation shows these techniques have efficient attack mitigation and secure energy transfer capabilities. The article concludes with recommendations for future research, urging the development of robust, scalable, and adaptive cyber security framework with respect to wireless EV charging frameworks in smart transportation ecosystems.

venue: 2026 International Conference on Electric Power and Renewable Energy (EPREC)
title: Cyber–Physical Power Systems: Attacks, Detection, and Cross-Domain Mitigation
abstract: The electrical grid’s evolution into an interconnected cyber–physical system has markedly increased its operational capabilities — and its exposure to malicious actors. This paper surveys major cyber threats across generation, transmission, distribution and device layers, then synthesizes a compact taxonomy of detection approaches ranging from physics-aware estimators to statistical and machine-learning detectors and timing-based monitors. Building on domain-specific examples (e.g., PMU manipulations, false data injection, firmware tampering and denial-of-service), we propose a layered detection architecture that integrates lightweight edge checks, local physics-consistency tests, central machine-learning ensembles, and timing integrity monitors. The proposed stack maps naturally onto the NIST Cybersecurity Framework functions (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover), providing a practical prioritization path for utilities. Finally, we identify open problems — adversarial robustness for ML detectors, low-latency authenticated protection messaging in IEC 61850 Type-1 services, and supply-chain provenance — and propose concrete near-term measures such as time-source redundancy, firmware signing, and PMU placement audits. The goal is a compact, implementable roadmap that balances rapid detection, operational latency constraints, and long-term resilience investments.

title: A Secure IoT and Machine Learning Framework using Variational Autoencoders for Intelligent Cyberattack Detection
abstract: The growing number of Internet of Things (IoT) smart ecosystems in the fields of smart healthcare, industrial automation, smart grids, and low-altitude UAV infrastructures has led to a greater exposure to attacks such as distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, port scanning, replay attacks, and zero-day intrusions. Current intrusion detection systems (IDS) for IoT networks tend to be supervised learning systems with poor generalization capabilities, and they also may demand a centralized aggregation of data that is difficult to operate in privacy-sensitive and resource-constrained settings in the edge. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces VAE-IoT CyberShield, an endowment of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and federated differential privacy, as well as edge-optimized inference for real-time IoT security analytics, to provide a lightweight and secure framework for detecting cyberattacks. The proposed framework first learns probabilistic latent representations of the normal network traffic, and then determines the anomalous behavior based on a threshold of the reconstruction error calculated using the Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) method. The federated training protocol with differential privacy keeps the sensitive traffic information safe when collaborating on model optimization. Experimental results on NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15, CIC-IoT2023 and Smart-Grid Telemetry datasets show that the proposed method achieves a mean detection accuracy of 97.4%, an F1-score of 0.971 and a false positive rate of 0.9%, which is superior to the state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised baselines. In addition, the compressed edge model has an inference latency of 2.1ms when running on ARM Cortex-M4 hardware, demonstrating its real-time capabilities for use in resource-constrained IoT applications.

abstract: An accurate forecasting of energy consumption is a core need of effective energy planning, smart grid operation, and sustainable energy management.
